How I Did It: Star Guardian

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

Defender showed up in '81 and about scared people off it — that control panel had five buttons and everybody's thumbs seized up the first week. I had one regular, a fella named Wallace, who swore up and down he was going to master "the one with the little people" before he turned forty. He did, eventually, and bought the whole bar a round the night he finally rescued every last humanoid on a single credit. Best quarter that machine ever earned him back a hundredfold in bragging rights.

What the remodel changed

This is the biggest one the crew and I built for this remodel — a whole world, four screens wide, that wraps clean around itself instead of stopping at an edge. The camera actually leans ahead of you now, the direction you're flying, instead of just sitting dead-center like a nervous passenger. I got a little radar strip up top so I can see the whole planet at once — where my people are, where the trouble is — same idea as the original, just redrawn clean. And the "juice," as the robots keep calling it: shake when I lose a ship, a flash and a fanfare when a wave clears, floating numbers over every rescue. Wallace would've lost his mind over the radar alone.

The spell that did it

Build Defender against our GZ engine. I want a real wrapping world, wider than the screen, with a camera that leads ahead of the ship instead of centering on it, plus a little radar strip across the top showing the whole planet. Landers grab humanoids off the ground and haul them up — let me shoot the lander to drop the humanoid, then catch it myself for the big rescue bonus, or carry it back down for even more. If I lose every last humanoid, let the planet crack and turn every lander loose as a mutant hunting me. Smart bomb clears the screen. Make every rescue and every kill feel like it mattered.

Under the hood

  • The whole planet is one number line, 3200 pixels around, and everything — the ship, the enemies, even the mountain silhouette itself — wraps on that same number using modulo math, so flying off the right edge just puts you back on the left with no seam.
  • The camera doesn't just follow the ship, it eases toward a point out ahead of it based on which way you're flying, so you can always see what's coming instead of what you just passed.
  • A humanoid mid-fall remembers how high it was when the lander first grabbed it — drop from too high without catching it and it doesn't survive the landing, same rules as the original.
  • Every distance check between the ship and anything else in the world has to measure the short way around the wrap, not just a straight subtraction, or things on opposite sides of the planet would look like they're right next to each other.
